newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Britain meets inflation target in April.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Britain meets inflation target in April.

text.p: Britain's former Conservative government met its inflation target in April, when the underlying annual rate dipped to 2.5 percent, according to official figures published on Thursday.

The Office for National Statistcs (ONS) said underlying inflation, excluding volatile mortgage interest payments, rose 0.6 percent in April compared with March, taking the annual rate down to 2.5 percent from 2.7 percent.
This was the lowest annual figure since November 1994, when underlying inflation was 2.3 percent.
The figures mean that former Prime Minister John Major's Conservatives, who had set an inflation target of 2.5 percent or less, achieved this goal in their last month in office.
Major was ousted when Labour leader Tony Blair won a landslide election victory on May 1.
"This morning's data confirm the view that, in the short run, inflationary pressures remain subdued in the UK," said Audrey Childe-Freeman, an economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.

The headline annual inflation rate was 2.4 percent in April, down from 2.6 percent in March. The ONS said the decline was largely due to lower motoring costs, with prices for vehicles, petrol and oil all falling in April.
The figures again showed an imbalance between goods, prices of which rose a modest 1.7 percent year-on-year, and services, where prices increased by a robust 3.3 percent.
"I don't think there are any worries about inflation in the traded goods sector," said Glenn Davies, chief economist at Credit Lyonnais.
"But if you look at services, that is the part of the economy that is growing very strongly at the moment. That's where I think the inflation worry really is."

Despite the favourable April numbers, most economists believe inflation is likely to head higher because of strong economic growth fuelled by rising high street spending, unless action is taken to dampen demand.

The new government raised official interest rates to 6.25 percent from 6.0 percent last week and the Bank of England warned this week that they would have to rise again if the 2.5 percent inflation target is to be met in the medium term.
Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown unexpectedly ceded the power to set interest rates to the central bank within days of taking office.
Alex Garrard, an economist at UBS, said there was no pressing need for the central bank to raise interest rates at the inaugural meeting of its new monetary policy committee next month.

"Nevertheless, the gradual tightening of conditions in the labour market, combined with our expectation that consumer demand will remain robust over the coming months, suggests that there will be a need for a modest further tightening of policy over the coming months," he said.
